name: Pyynikin näkötorni
imageCredit: Photo: Tiia Monto / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0
hint: Follow the forest paths uphill to the ridge. A café famous for its doughnuts sits at the foot of this tower.
info: Completed in 1929, this 26-metre observation tower was built from local red granite. Its position on top of the Pyynikki ridge gives visitors views towards both Näsijärvi and Pyhäjärvi. The tower opened in the year of Tampere's 150th anniversary.

name: Hatanpään arboretum
imageCredit: Photo: Tiia Monto / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0
hint: Look for garden paths and a small footbridge near the shore of Pyhäjärvi, south of Hatanpää Manor.
info: Planting at Hatanpää Arboretum began in 1973. Most of the arboretum was created on land built up with imported soil along the lakeshore. Its rock garden was added in 1994.

name: Lielahden kartano
imageCredit: Photo: Juha Laaksoharju / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0
hint: Head towards the shore of Näsijärvi beside the old factory area. Look for a red-brick manor surrounded by parkland.
info: The manor's main building was completed in 1893 during the von Nottbeck family's ownership. The estate once included a huge cowshed and a private railway seven kilometres long. In 1913, a new owner began transforming the estate into a pulp mill complex.

name: Tampereen tuomiokirkko
imageCredit: Photo: Tiia Monto / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0
hint: Look just north of the railway station for a stone church with red roofs, surrounded by a small park.
info: Designed by Lars Sonck and completed in 1907, Tampere Cathedral represents Finland's National Romantic architecture. Inside are frescoes by Hugo Simberg, including The Wounded Angel and The Garden of Death. His ceiling painting of a winged serpent caused controversy when the church was new.

name: Kalevan kirkko
imageCredit: Photo: kallerna / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0
hint: Look for a tall, pale church on Liisankallio hill, beside the park between Teiskontie and Sammonkatu.
info: Designed by Reima and Raili Pietilä, Kaleva Church opened in 1966. Its curved shape was inspired by the fish, an early Christian symbol. Inside, the worship space rises 30 metres high, with tall windows bringing natural light into the building.

name: Halimasjärvi
imageCredit: Photo: J Hokkanen / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0
hint: Look east of Atala for a small lake enclosed by forest. A path from the end of Sompakatu leads towards its shoreline trail and boardwalks.
info: The forests around Halimasjärvi were first protected in 1988, and the reserve was expanded in 2013. Much of the woodland consists of mature spruce forest, with fallen trees left to support fungi and insects. Red-throated divers regularly nest on the lake, while bats hunt along its shores after dusk.

name: Näsilinna
imageCredit: Photo: Tiia Monto / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0
hint: Climb the paths of Näsinpuisto, just north of the Finlayson factory area, and look for the palace on the hill.
info: Completed in 1898, this Neo-Baroque palace was originally named Milavida. Peter von Nottbeck commissioned it, and architect Karl August Wrede designed the building. The palace connects Tampere's industrial history with the wealthy family behind the Finlayson cotton factory.

name: Suolioja
imageCredit: Photo: Aulis Eskola / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 4.0
hint: West of Hervanta, look for a narrow forest stream connecting two lakes. One lake's name begins with Särki, the other with Suoli.
info: Suolioja carries water from Särkijärvi into Suolijärvi through the forest west of Hervanta. Its width varies along the route, narrowing in places to a small woodland stream. The water eventually continues through lakes in neighbouring Lempäälä towards Pyhäjärvi.

name: Kampusareena — Tampere University
imageCredit: Photo: Kotivalo / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0
hint: Find Kampusareena on Korkeakoulunkatu, in the middle of the university campus.
info: Kampusareena has a green roof that even includes insect hotels. The Hervanta campus began taking shape when its first building, Konetalo, was completed in 1973.

name: Tahmelan huvila
imageCredit: Photo: Aulis Eskola / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0
hint: Look for a wooden villa at the lakeside end of Uramonkatu, beside Pyhäjärvi.
info: Tahmelan huvila was built as a summer villa in the 1890s on land belonging to Harjupispa farm. It is also known as Tahmelanniemen huvila or Pispan huvila.

name: Kirkkokiven laavu
imageCredit: Photo: Aulis Eskola / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0
hint: In Kintulammi's forest, follow the short accessible trail from the P1 parking area. Look for a steep-roofed wooden shelter near a large boulder.
info: Designed by architect Malin Moisio and completed in 2018, this woodland shelter takes its name from a nearby glacial boulder. According to local tradition, horse herders used the boulder as a church in the 1700s. Openings in the shelter's wooden walls frame small views of the surrounding forest.
